items.gist: Śakti sustains creation; the guru properly sets it in motion for Kula ends. The procedure is then to be carried out in people through their own bodies.
Kallaṭanātha's statement is cited for obtaining the whole meaning. The tradition is received mouth to mouth, and knowledge is thereby attained.
In the two created realms, those established in the unbroken visarga-pada seek attainment. They worship the arisen form with pure consciousness-nearness.
Those not yet awakened perform the arisen, blossoming rite. Through the Śakti-cakra and bliss-rasa they attain knowledge.
The practitioner worships the gaṇas and deities in the four directions according to rule. The raśmi-cakra and varied eightfold groupings are also worshipped.
The quiet form is practiced in one's own bodily abode. Resting in that quiet state, all cakra deities become inactive and blissless.
Even those who possess subordinate-cakra forms depend on that state. The sense-rays remain without own form, seeking bliss and union.
After obtaining a resting abode, one offers into oneself. The cakra-lord is then aroused by the previously stated method.
Emission is threefold: union, arisen, and quiet. The sources describe kuṇḍa, Śakti, Śiva, liṅga, and supreme union.
Rest, absorption, and the removal of distinctions occur in the body's seventy-two places and crown. Śiva unites coming and going there.
One should remain in the Bhairava-state of union. One practices awareness free from measure-division and all conceptual constructions.
Sun and moon are restrained along the path of dissolution and dispersion. The resulting resonance is mantra-power, eager for its fruit.
One performs japa there, entering single-cakra awareness. The supreme mudrā beloved of yoginīs is described through nāda.
The lotus with sixteen petals and central stem is set in fire. Through the union of moon, sun, and red power, creation arises.
Performing creation and so forth inwardly in the fourth state, one attains stability. In enjoyment and laughter, mantra-power arises through unbroken resonances.
The eightfold Bhairava pada is attained in the supreme abode. The eightfold nāda-Bhairava arises from the union of two cakras.
The pervasion made of light and sound is called supreme. It is free from all kalās and impurities, and pervades through various bodily locations.
One who is always unsoiled becomes a living liberated being. Even a child in the womb is said to be Śiva-form.
The essence is taken from the principal rite, hence it is called ādiyāga. Its form is praised in various scriptures.
Without vow or yoga, one constantly remembers the ādiyāga. One places the vidyā in one's own Śakti-body in due order.
One meditates on the moon-like lotus and sun-like self, uniting the two pīṭhas. The secret is not plainly taught, but indicated to the curious.
The cakra is the supreme deity, and the body itself is the supreme liṅga. The maṇḍala is worshipped both outside and within.
One touches with blissful essences according to the rite. The awakened consciousness-cakra obtains the supreme abode, and inner satisfaction follows.
One worships Devī with the god in the bodily temple with blissful offerings. This is praised as the supreme rite in the Vīrāvalī tradition.
Alternatively, the guru sees all deities established in prāṇa and worships them there. By prāṇa-order tarpaṇa, knowledge and powers are quickly attained.
